title: Those closest
hookLine: love at home is where faith is tested most
tomorrow: a kid asks a God question from the back seat. now what?

cards: A customer service voice: patient, warm, endlessly polite. Then the call ends, someone at home asks where the charger went, and that voice is gone. Strangers get the good hour.
Home gets every hour, including the tired ones. So why is kindness hardest exactly where love is supposed to live?

teach.b: Because home is where love is tested over time, and the Bible describes love in just those terms. Paul writes: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up.”
Charity is the King James word for love. Suffereth long: patience that only gets tested where people live close.

teach.h: THE BROTHER WHOM HE HATH SEEN.
teach.b: And John is blunt about the order: “he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?” The person you've seen comes first. Now a neighbor who says it too.

teach.h: A NEIGHBOR: BEST TO THEIR FAMILIES.
teach.b: In Islam, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded by al-Tirmidhi, runs like this in paraphrase: the best of you are those who are best to their families, and he is the best of them to his own.
Muslims hear it as part of his example. The same instinct: kindness that never reaches home isn't finished. And one honest difference.
John makes love for the person in front of you the test of love for God. The hadith makes it the measure of a person's goodness, and points to the Prophet's own conduct at home.
Two neighbors at the same kitchen table, each listening to their own teacher. Home doesn't have to mean family by blood; it's whoever shares your days.
And love at home never means staying in danger. If home isn't safe, reach out to local emergency help.

how: Christians practice love at home in small daily ways, such as patience, shared chores, a blessing at meals or bedtime; Muslims look to the Prophet's example at home, recalling his saying that the best of people are the best to their families.

o: the relatives you're closest to by blood, and no one else
the people who share your days, where love is tested most
the friends you choose in place of your family

games.q: love at home, two neighbors — tap the pairs.
p: the King James word for love
the brother whom he hath seen
best of you, best to their families

s: in the KJV's 1 Corinthians 13, charity means giving to the poor
it's the King James word for love: charity suffereth long, and is kind.
1 John ties loving God unseen to loving the brother you've seen
"how can he love God whom he hath not seen?"
Christianity and Islam say this about family in exactly the same way
both put love at home first. John makes it a test of loving God; the hadith a measure of goodness, with the Prophet's example.

games.q: you've been calm all day at work and with friends. you get home and your brother's music is blasting. what does 'suffereth long' look like?
o: save the patience for people who don't know you yet.
ask kindly once, and let the small stuff go.
never say anything; love means never naming a problem.
games.why: Paul's love suffers long and is kind, and isn't easily provoked. at home that's often small: one kind ask, then patience.

practice: By hand, write the name of one person you live with or are closest to, and beside it one small kindness they'd notice: a chore done before it's asked, a real hello at the door.
Rest the paper in your lap for the sit, and if you pray, hold their name there.

wordCard.voice: Those closest. The people who share your days, where love is tested most and proved in small things.

orig.note: Greek: love, the word the KJV renders charity in 1 Corinthians 13.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: love begins at home, at the counter and the door. Day seventeen-fourteen, and the kitchen counts.
